title: Billionaire Bill Ackman Says There’s a Huge Disconnect in Wall Street’s Expectations for Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, and Alphabet
detail:
Billionaire Bill Ackman Says There’s a Huge Disconnect in Wall Street’s Expectations for Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, and Alphabet
Adam Levy, The Motley Fool

The stock market hasn't been as keen on the hyperscalers in 2026 as it was in years past. Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) have delivered better returns than the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) year to date thanks to strong relative performances over the past month or so. Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) and Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) haven't fared nearly as well — they're down for the year.

But that could be an opportunity for long-term retail investors. Billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman believes the market has soured on these four stocks due to a "notable disconnect" between market expectations and the businesses' fundamentals. That's reflected in growing skepticism among analysts that the massive amounts these companies are spending on new data centers will yield meaningful returns on investment.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

But the actual financial results and management's commentary should give investors confidence that the future may be brighter for these hyperscalers than the average analyst expects.

Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman. Image source: Getty Images.

The huge disconnect on Wall Street

In his third-quarter letter to Pershing Square shareholders, Ackman expressed his belief that most analysts aren't properly accounting for the potential revenue growth stemming from the stepped-up capital spending among Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, and Alphabet. He wrote:

Consensus analyst estimates for the hyperscalers reflect a notable disconnect: they expect the current level of capital intensity to persist for years into the future, yet they assume minimal acceleration in revenue growth beyond this year and next. Consensus estimates treat the capex buildout as a structural increase in maintenance capital intensity rather than as an investment capable of producing outsized future revenue growth and attractive returns on capital.

That is to say, Wall Street is acting like the increase in capital expenditures won't result in a commensurate increase in revenue over time. That's despite the fact that their prior spending has already been doing so for all four hyperscalers.

Meta, notably, saw accelerating growth in its advertising business as it accelerated its capital expenditures. And with the potential to grow its Muse agentic AI service, expand business messaging, and collect licensing revenue from its large language models (LLMs), it could see a sharp rise in direct artificial intelligence monetization in the near future.

Key Takeaways

Whale Rock Capital, a hedge fund firm managing nearly $13 billion, sold all its Astera Labs, Carvana and Western Digital stock in the third quarter while building up Meta and SiTime.

Astera Labs and Western Digital are each down 54% since June 30, the last date the fund reported owning them, while Carvana is up 10%.

Analysts' average targets sit 55% above Astera Labs' price and 107% above Western Digital's, but just 13% above Carvana's.

Astera Labs looks like the sale most worth second-guessing, and Carvana the one to leave sold.

A $13 billion hedge fund just cleaned out three stocks, and two of them have fallen by more than half since it last reported owning them.

Whale Rock Capital's 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 13, shows no shares left of Astera Labs (ALAB:NASDAQ), Carvana (CVNA:NYSE) or Western Digital (WDC:NASDAQ). Meanwhile, it more than doubled its Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) stake, now its largest at 7.6% of its 13F stocks, and added a third to SiTime (SITM:NASDAQ).

A 13F doesn't say when in the quarter a fund sold, what it got, or why. But it does flag three stocks worth a second look.

Astera Labs' growth hasn't gone anywhere

Astera Labs was Whale Rock's biggest exit: 1.57 million shares on June 30, worth $757 million, or 6.1% of its 13F stocks then. The stock is down 54% since, even though the business is still growing fast. Third-quarter revenue rose 154% to $584.9 million, and management guided the fourth quarter well above what analysts expected, at $730 million to $750 million. The worry is breadth: Scorpio X switches shipped to just two customers in the quarter, and CFO Desmond Lynch said on the call that "the initial Scorpio X platforms have completed much of their initial deployment ramps." Management expects new customers to get only pre-production shipments this quarter.

Carvana kept climbing

Carvana went the other way. Whale Rock held 4.27 million shares on June 30, worth $281 million, or 2.3% of its 13F stocks, and the stock is up 10% since.

Sales are booming. Carvana sold a record 217,385 retail cars in the third quarter, up 39%, and now expects full-year adjusted EBITDA at the higher end of $2.7 billion to $3.0 billion. But profit per car keeps slipping: adjusted EBITDA per car fell to about $3,680 from $4,085 a year earlier, its fourth straight year-over-year decline. Not every fund agrees with Whale Rock here: 16 big funds bought Carvana.

title: Will ETF Buying Change Meta Stock Narrative
detail:
Will ETF Buying Change Meta Stock Narrative
Al Bentley
Fri, November 13, 2026 at 4:20 PM PST 4 min read
META
SPY
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Large ETFs including SPY, XLC and SPYM recently added to Meta Platforms positions over several days, alongside fresh fixed income offerings and expanded sustainability agreements tied to green steel, clean cement and zero emission trucking.

The combination of strong ETF buying and growing use of AI to sharpen Meta Platforms advertising engine reinforces how central data driven ad performance remains to the business story, even as it layers on heavy capex and new financing to fund AI and infrastructure.

We will now look at how strong ETF inflows into Meta Platforms interact with its AI commerce thesis and capex heavy roadmap.

Surf 53 AI infrastructure stocks, which, like Meta Platforms, are raising serious capital for data centers and AI capacity, and see which issuers are drawing the most attention right now.

Meta Platforms Investment Narrative Recap

Owning Meta Platforms means buying into the idea, outlined by mitchell_lawler, a Simply Wall St Community investor who wrote the Narrative, that its AI powered ad engine can evolve into a toll on commerce built on more than 3.5 billion daily users. In the short term, the key driver remains ad performance on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp and whether AI driven targeting keeps supporting revenue and profit growth.

The biggest near term risk sits in the scale and financing of that AI and data center build. Recent bond deals and equity issuance lift funding costs and scrutiny of returns, but do not change the core near term catalyst, which is whether advertisers keep directing budgets toward Meta inventory.

The IMAX Enhanced certification for upcoming Meta VR glasses and the planned IMAX app for a virtual theatre experience show Reality Labs still getting real product and content partners. For shareholders, that matters less as a potential 2027 revenue driver and more as a proof point that Meta is still investing in use cases around attention and premium video.

That VR tie up also sits alongside heavy capex, legal settlements and large bond offerings, which together raise the execution bar. If AI infrastructure and immersive hardware eventually channel more commerce and entertainment back into Meta's ads ecosystem, investors may see a clearer path for those capital commitments to support the catalysts highlighted by mitchell_lawler around AI driven conversion gains.

Using revenue growth of 14.0% a year and a future profit margin of 40.0%, mitchell_lawler frames Meta Platforms as a potential toll on commerce, and on those assumptions the Narrative arrives at a fair value of US$1,019 per share.
